q: What reason is given for a full verification node to exist?
options: Anyone who accepts bitcoins has a strong incentive to verify what they receive
Banks require every merchant to run one before accepting any bitcoin payment
Mining rewards are paid only to the operators of nodes that verify the whole chain themselves
The network stops working once fewer than a thousand nodes remain online
why: People accept money only if they believe they can spend it later, so everyone who accepts bitcoins has an incentive to verify the integrity of what they receive.

q: What question do the four concepts of the verification group answer together?
options: How a miner decides which transactions go first inside a new block
How much disk space a node needs before its first download can finish
How a participant can be sure that what the software enforces is what Bitcoin requires
How a user can recover coins after losing the file that holds the keys
why: The group names the program that checks the rules, the model program, the documents that record the rules and the soft fork that changes them.

q: Why does a user who runs a full node have to trust less than one who asks another server?
options: The node is run by the miner of the block, so the miner no longer needs trust
The node checks blocks against public rules, so only the software and the rules need trust
The node encrypts every payment, so no outside party can see any amount
The node keeps the user's keys offline in a separate device, so a stolen password cannot move coins
why: A user who relies on someone else's server has to trust that server, while a full node verifies everything itself and the rules are public.

q: A pruned node deletes old block files. Is it still a full node, and why?
options: No, a node that has discarded any block can no longer validate what it receives
Yes, but only after a lightweight client confirms each block that was deleted
No, because the word full means that every block is stored forever
Yes, it still verifies the whole chain and only keeps the most recent blocks
why: The word full is not a promise about storage: a pruned node verified the whole chain but keeps only recent blocks.

q: What does the term reference implementation mean when Mastering Bitcoin applies it to Bitcoin Core?
options: It is the only program that may connect to the peer-to-peer network
It provides a reference for how each part of the technology should be implemented
It is the written specification from which the other programs are automatically generated
It is the first program Satoshi Nakamoto ran on a private test network
why: The book calls Bitcoin Core the reference implementation because it provides a reference for how each part of the technology should be implemented.

q: Why is it said that the code of Bitcoin Core alone does not define Bitcoin?
options: The whitepaper and the BIPs document the rules too, so documents and code describe them together
Each release changes the rules, so the documents only record versions that are gone
Most nodes run other programs, so those programs and not Bitcoin Core are the ones that set the rules
The code is kept private, so the public can read only the BIPs about the design
why: Early parts are described in the whitepaper and most major parts since 2011 in BIPs, so the written documents and the code together describe the rules.

q: Who assigns the number of a new BIP, according to the process document that governed BIPs from 2016?
options: The author, who takes the next free number when opening the pull request
The miners, who signal the number in the version field of their blocks
The maintainers of Bitcoin Core, when they merge the code for the proposal
A BIP editor, because authors must not assign numbers to themselves
why: The process document says that a BIP editor assigns the number and that authors must not assign numbers to themselves.

q: What does this program print for the preamble of BIP 9?
code:
headers = {'BIP': '9', 'Status': 'Deployed', 'Type': 'Informational'}
print('bip%s' % headers['BIP'], headers['Status'].upper())
options: BIP9 deployed
bip 9 Deployed
bip9 DEPLOYED
bip9 INFORMATIONAL
why: The format string builds the name bip9 from the number, and the status Deployed is converted to upper case.

q: What property makes a change to the consensus rules a soft fork?
options: Older nodes reject every block that newer nodes create, so all of them must upgrade at once
Newer nodes may reject blocks that older nodes accept, but never the other way round
The change is voted on by users, and the network splits if the vote fails
Old and new nodes accept exactly the same blocks, so no new rule is enforced
why: The book defines the property: nodes with the change must not accept blocks that nodes without it would consider invalid.

q: Which of these block versions signal a BIP 9 deployment, as this program decides?
code:
versions = [0x20000000, 0x20000002, 0x00000001, 0x3FFFFFFF]
print([v >> 29 == 1 for v in versions])
options: [True, True, True, True]
[True, False, False, True]
[False, True, False, False]
[True, True, False, True]
why: Shifting right by 29 bits leaves the top three bits, which must be 001, so only the version 1 is not signalling.

q: Which two concepts does the project group contain?
options: Full node and reference implementation of the protocol
Initial download and pruned node
Open-source software and Satoshi Nakamoto
Release tag and git repository
why: The project group contains open-source software, the form of publication, and Satoshi Nakamoto, the origin.

q: Which conditions besides access to the source code does the Open Source Initiative's definition require?
options: Free redistribution, included source code, and permission for modifications and derived works
Payment of a royalty, a registered trademark and a signed contributor agreement for each change
Approval by a foundation, a fixed release schedule and a public list of bugs
An unmodified binary, a warranty from the authors and a ban on resale
why: The definition says that open source does not just mean access to source code and lists these distribution terms.

q: Why does open source code not prove that a downloaded program was built from it?
options: Open code is compiled differently on every machine, so no two builds can ever match
The MIT license forbids anyone from publishing a program built from the code
Only the master branch is open, while the release versions are kept private by the maintainers
Openness concerns the code, so a release must still be checked with checksums and signatures
why: Openness of the source does not by itself prove that a download was built from it, so the ecosystem branch explains checksums, signatures and reproducible builds.

q: What does the name Satoshi Nakamoto stand for, according to Mastering Bitcoin?
options: A pseudonym of the person or people who designed Bitcoin, whose real identity is unknown
The company that sells the reference implementation and holds the trademark on the name Bitcoin
The mining pool that found the first block of the blockchain
The committee elected to maintain the code of Bitcoin Core
why: The glossary says the real identity of Satoshi Nakamoto remains unknown, and the history chapter calls the name an alias.

q: What happened in April 2011 that Mastering Bitcoin mentions?
options: Nakamoto published the whitepaper and the first release of the software together
Nakamoto handed control of the network to a foundation of miners
Nakamoto withdrew from the public and left development to a group of volunteers
Nakamoto revealed an identity in a statement signed with the first key
why: The book states that Nakamoto withdrew from the public in April 2011, leaving development to a group of volunteers.

q: On which day of the week does the Unix time of the first block fall in this program?
code:
from datetime import datetime, timezone
print(datetime.fromtimestamp(1231006505, timezone.utc).strftime('%A %Y-%m-%d'))
options: Saturday 2009-01-03
Saturday 2008-12-31
why: The Unix time 1231006505 is the third of January 2009 in UTC, and the program also prints the weekday.

q: Why does the course read the figures of the resource group against the date of their source?
options: They are set by the protocol and change only at a halving
They apply only to nodes that run on a metered connection
They are orders of magnitude that change from year to year and are not constants
They were measured on test networks and not on the main network
why: The group says that its figures are orders of magnitude that change from year to year.

q: In what order does a new node fetch data during the initial download, according to Mastering Bitcoin?
options: Full blocks first, then the headers once all of them have been validated
The set of unspent outputs first, then the blocks that created each output
Only the latest blocks first, then older ones whenever a peer asks for them
Headers first, to find the chain with most proof of work, then the blocks, validated on arrival
why: The book says the node first fetches the headers from peers to find the chain with the most proof of work, then downloads and validates the full blocks.

q: How much data must a node fetch after being off for ten days at the rate of 400 MB a day given in Mastering Bitcoin?
code:
daily, days = 400, 10
print(daily * days, 'MB', daily * days / 1000, 'GB')
options: 400 MB 0.4 GB
40 MB 0.04 GB
why: Ten days of 400 MB make 4000 MB, which divided by 1000 is the 4 GB the book names.

q: What does a pruned node give up in exchange for needing far less disk space?
options: It can no longer hand old blocks to other nodes
It stops verifying new blocks and trusts the peers that send them
It loses the set of unspent outputs and rebuilds it for each payment
It must connect to a single trusted peer that stores the full chain
why: A pruned node still verifies, but it deleted old blocks and so cannot serve them to other nodes.

q: What mode does each value of the prune option select in this program?
options: ['off', 'manual', 'auto', 'auto']
['off', 'manual', 'manual', 'auto']
['off', 'auto', 'auto', 'auto']
['manual', 'manual', 'auto', 'auto']
why: Zero disables pruning, one allows manual pruning, and any value from 550 up deletes files automatically to stay under that size in MiB.

q: How many connections does a node use when inbound connections are disabled, according to Bitcoin Core's guide to reducing memory?
options: No more than 125, as set by the option maxconnections
Exactly 8, all of them full-relay connections
No more than 11: 8 full-relay, 2 block-relay-only and occasionally 1 short-lived feeler
No more than 2, both of them block-relay-only connections
why: The guide says that without inbound connections the number is not more than 11, of which 8 are full-relay, 2 are block-relay-only and occasionally 1 is a feeler.

q: Why can a node safely connect to strangers as peers?
options: It accepts only peers whose addresses are on a list signed by the developers
Peers may send only block headers, which cannot change the chain of the node
The default limit of connections stops untrusted peers from ever forming a majority
It checks everything a peer sends against the rules, so a peer is not a trusted party
why: Everything a peer sends is checked by the receiving node against the rules, which is why a node can connect to strangers at all.

q: How many regular outgoing connections and how many in all does this program count?
code:
full_relay, block_only, feeler = 8, 2, 1
print(full_relay + block_only, full_relay + block_only + feeler)
why: Eight full-relay and two block-relay-only connections make ten, and the occasional feeler makes eleven.

q: Why does a node keep the set of unspent outputs instead of searching the whole history?
options: The set stores every wallet balance, so one lookup gives the amount owned
The history is deleted again once the node has downloaded it, so only the set remains
The set holds all signatures, so scripts never have to be run a second time
To check a transaction it only has to know whether each output it spends is in the set
why: A node does not need to search the history: it needs to know whether each output being spent is in the set, which is much smaller than the chain.

q: Why is the set of unspent outputs not a list of balances?
options: It holds only the outputs of the wallet in the node, and a wallet has a single balance
It holds outputs, and what a wallet owns is the sum of the outputs it can spend
It is stored inside each block header, so a separate list of balances would duplicate it
It is rebuilt for each block, so no amount stays stored between two blocks
why: The set holds outputs; the amount a wallet owns is the sum of those it can spend.

q: What set of outputs is left by this program after the transaction is verified?
why: Verifying the transaction removes the spent outpoint and adds the two new ones, so one entry leaves and two enter, leaving three.

q: Why do the printed build commands of Mastering Bitcoin fail on a current source tree?
options: Release 29.0 migrated the build from Autotools to CMake, and the tree has no autogen.sh
The project left GitHub, so the cloning command of the book finds nothing
The source is now written in Python only, so no compiler is needed for the build of the program
Git no longer allows a release tag to be checked out in a detached state
why: The commands belong to a build system that was replaced in release 29.0, and the current tree has a top-level CMakeLists.txt and no autogen.sh.

q: What does the source group give a learner the means to say exactly?
options: Which compiler options were used to build the version that is currently running
Which miners have accepted the rules of the version in question
Which wallet file belongs to the version that is installed
Which version of the program is meant, through repository, tag and suffix
why: A repository holds every version, a tag names one of them, and a suffix tells whether it is meant for testing.

q: What does a release tag attach a version number to?
options: One configuration file of the node that is currently running
One signature made by the lead maintainer
One specific snapshot of the code repository
One block of the blockchain
why: A release tag is a name that the developers attach to one specific snapshot of the code repository to mark a release.

q: Why is checking out a tag not by itself proof that the maintainers released the code?
options: Tags are created automatically by GitHub and not by the developers
A tag is only a label, and signatures and reproducible builds are what show who made it
A checked-out tag leaves the working files empty until a build is run
Tags name branches, which keep changing after the checkout is done
why: A tag is a label, not a guarantee; trust in a release comes from the signatures and reproducible builds described in the ecosystem branch.

q: What do the version number and the client version come to in this program for the tag v24.0.1?
code:
major, minor, build = 24, 0, 1
print('v%d.%d.%d' % (major, minor, build), 10000 * major + 100 * minor + build)
why: The client version is 10000 times the major number plus 100 times the minor number plus the build number, which is 240001.

q: In which languages are the main program and the regression tests of Bitcoin Core written?
options: The program in Python and the tests in C++
The program in C++ and the regression and integration tests in Python
The program in Java and the tests in the shell
Both in C, with no other language used
why: The build notes call the main language C++ and the readme says the regression and integration tests are written in Python.

q: Why is the source code the most exact description of the rules a node enforces?
options: The whitepaper and the proposals describe only parts, and the code settles the rest
It is the only text signed by the maintainers, while the documents have no signature
The whitepaper was removed after the first release, so the code is all that is left
The proposals are rewritten with each release, so they cannot be cited by number
why: The whitepaper describes several early parts and the proposals later ones, but questions such as how much money a block may create are answered finally by reading the code.

q: What block subsidy in the smallest unit does this program print for height 420000?
why: Height 420000 lies in the third era, after two halvings, so the starting 5,000,000,000 is shifted right by two bits.

q: What is true of the repository on a user's machine after the command git clone?
options: It holds only the latest snapshot and fetches older ones on demand
It stays a live view and updates itself when the maintainers add tags
It contains the compiled programs of each release but not the source code of tagged releases
It holds the whole history and is as complete as the original on the hosting service
why: Every copy contains the whole history, and the clone is a snapshot of one moment that does not update by itself.

q: Why does the name of a commit change when its content changes in any way?
options: Git numbers the commits in order and renumbers them after every change
The hosting service assigns the names and assigns new ones after a change
The maintainers sign every commit with a new key after each change
Git names each commit by a hash computed from its content
why: A commit identifier is an application of a hash function, so any change of the content changes the name.

q: What does this program print for the full commit name and its abbreviation to nine characters?

32 05bc2f53c True

q: Which rule does Mastering Bitcoin give for choosing a release to compile?
options: Choose the highest version without a suffix
Choose the highest version with the suffix rc
Choose the oldest version in the list of tags
Choose the last tag of the list, whatever its name
why: Release candidates are for testing, so the book says to choose the highest version without a suffix, the one meant for production.

q: Which two concepts of the toolchain group are generations of build system?
options: The compilation and the executables
The build prerequisites and the bitcoin command
The Autotools build and the CMake build
The CMake build and the bitcoin command
why: The Autotools build is the one the book describes and the CMake build is in use since release 29.0.

q: What does the script configure do when a required library is missing?
options: It ends with an error instead of creating the build scripts
It downloads and installs the library before it goes on
It builds the program without the library and only gives a warning later
It switches to the CMake build for the rest of the run
why: The book says that configure terminates with an error if any library is missing or incompatible, and that it is run again after installing the prerequisite.

q: At which position does make come in this list of the Autotools commands, and what is the last one?

options: 2 make check
3 make check

3 sudo make install
why: The commands run in the order autogen.sh, configure, make, make check and sudo make install, so make is third and the install is last.

q: Which commands does the project's build guide give for the CMake build?
options: ./autogen.sh, then ./configure, then make
cmake -B build, then cmake --build build, then optionally cmake --install build
cmake --install build, then cmake -B build, then make check
make cmake, then make build, then make install
why: The build notes give these three commands, with the install step optional.

q: Why is an option copied from an Autotools tutorial usually useless with CMake?
options: CMake ignores every option and always builds the complete program
CMake accepts only options for the graphical client
The options were moved into the configuration file of the node
Option names belong to the build system, and CMake takes variables such as -DENABLE_WALLET=OFF
why: An option written for Autotools is silently useless to CMake, which has its own variables.

q: What does this program map the two Autotools options to?

['-DENABLE_WALLET=OFF', '-DBUILD_GUI=OFF']
['default', 'default']
['-DENABLE_WALLET=ON', 'default']
why: Disabling the wallet has a CMake variable, while leaving out the graphical client is now the default and needs no option.

q: What does bitcoin rpc stand for according to the help text?
options: A start of the node, equivalent to running bitcoind
A call of an RPC method, equivalent to running bitcoin-cli -named
A run of the wallet tool, equivalent to bitcoin-wallet
A start of the graphical client, equivalent to running bitcoin-qt directly
why: The help text lists rpc as calling an RPC method, equivalent to bitcoin-cli -named.

q: Why was a single front-door command introduced in release 30.0?
options: It replaces the node by a lighter program that skips verification
It is required to run a node, since bitcoind was removed from the release archive for good
It hides the planned split into processes, so users need not learn new binary names
It lets the user choose between Autotools and CMake at start-up
why: The project plans to split the software into separate processes, and a front door that chooses the binary spares users from learning new names.

q: What does this program print for the rpc command and the number of known commands?

q: Why can an interrupted compilation be resumed by typing make again?
options: Make keeps a copy of the whole machine state and restores it on the next start
Each source file is compiled independently into an object file, so finished files need not be redone
The compiler runs on servers of the project, which keep the result for the next request
Make skips the compilation and links the object files that were left over from the previous release
why: Each source file becomes an object file on its own and a final step links them, so the process can be interrupted and resumed.

q: What does a successful compilation show, and what does it leave open?
options: It shows that the program behaves correctly, so the tests may be skipped before installing
It shows that the release was signed by the maintainers, but not that it can run
The program was built, but not that it behaves correctly, which the unit tests check
It shows that every library on the computer has the version the project tested
why: A successful compilation shows that the program was built and not that it works, which is why the book tells the reader to run the unit tests before installing.

q: Which object files are still to be built in this program after an interruption?
options: ['net.o', 'wallet.o']
['main.o']
['net.o', 'wallet.o', 'main.o', 'rpc.o']
['main.o', 'rpc.o']
why: Only the files that were not finished before the interruption are compiled again, as when make is typed a second time.

gcc, git, curl and openssl

options: Qt is part of the compiler and always comes with build-essential
The interface depends on the wallet database, which is skipped when the wallet is switched off
The graphical client is the part that needs Qt, and it is not built by default
Qt is needed only for the tests, which the default build leaves out

q: Which executable of Bitcoin Core creates and modifies transactions?
options: bitcoin-util
bitcoin-wallet
bitcoin-cli
bitcoin-tx
why: The documentation describes bitcoin-tx as the tool for creating and modifying transactions.

q: Why does the client bitcoin-cli not contain the node?
options: It copies the chain from the data directory of the node before it runs each command
It starts the node as a second process and stops it after the command
It contains the node but exposes only the wallet functions to the user
It connects to a running node over the network interface and sends it commands
why: The client connects to a running node over the network interface and sends commands, so it is a separate small program.

q: How many executables are in each folder of the release 31.1 archive, and is test_bitcoin in bin?
options: 7 3 True

q: What does a package manager do that installing the prerequisites by hand does not?
options: It compiles the program with the compiler options that the operator of the node has chosen
It checks the signature of every block it downloads for the node
It installs a package together with everything the package depends on, using one command
It replaces the build system and so makes the build step unnecessary
why: A package manager finds the packages and resolves which other libraries are needed, instead of the builder downloading and compiling each.

q: Why does the project also offer a way to build the dependencies from source?
options: A package manager trusts the collection it installs from, and a security-critical program should limit that trust
Distribution packages never include libraries, so a builder must compile them
Package names are the same everywhere, so only a source build can differ
Source builds are faster than installing packages, which matters for a node
why: A package manager installs what the distribution maintainers packaged, so the project offers the depends system for building the dependencies from source.

q: Which three groups does the operation branch have?
options: Source, toolchain and executables
Transactions, blocks and chain state
Checksums, signatures and registries
Configuration, running and wallet
why: The operation branch explains configuration of the node, running it, and the wallet that comes with it.

q: Where does the node look for its configuration file?
options: In its data directory, on every start
In the folder of the executables, but only on the first start
On the network, from the first peer it connects to
In the build directory, where CMake wrote its cache
why: The book says that Bitcoin Core looks for a configuration file in its data directory on every start.

q: Which format does the configuration file use?
options: A JSON object with one key for each option and one for comments
One option=value entry per line, without the leading hyphen of the command line
One -option value pair per line, with the hyphen kept
A table of rows in which the option name stands in square brackets and the value in braces
why: The documentation describes entries of the form option=value, one per line, written without the hyphen used on the command line.

q: Why can a mistyped option name in the configuration file go unnoticed?
options: The program quietly replaces it with the nearest option name that it knows
Only the graphical client reads the file, and it does not report names
An unknown option is not an error but only a warning in the log
Changes take effect at once, so the next line overwrites the mistake
why: An option that the program does not know shows up as a warning in the log, so nobody notices if the log is not read.

q: Which value is used when an option is set both in the file and on the command line?
options: The file value, because the node reads the file last
The larger of the two numbers, whatever source it came from
Neither, because the program refuses to start when an option is given twice
The command-line value, because it overrides the value in the file
why: The documentation states that command-line options override values set in the configuration file.

q: What does the prefix no in front of an option name do?
options: It marks the option as a comment that the program ignores
It negates the option, which in general sets a boolean or numeric option to zero
It restricts the option to the test network
It marks the option as valid on the command line only
why: Almost all options can be negated with the prefix no, and a line with that prefix is not a typing error.

q: Where is the default data directory on Linux?

A folder named bitcoin inside /usr/local/bin
A folder named .bitcoin in the home directory of the user
A folder named data next to the executables
why: The documentation and the book give the .bitcoin folder in the home directory for Linux.

q: Why must a wallet file not be copied between running nodes?
options: A wallet file is tied to one network, so the copy would be empty
The second node would not start without the lock file of the first
The wallet is stored in a format that only the very node that wrote it is able to read
It can result in key reuse and double spends, so the backup call should be used
